headline: Cape May Rips Grade: C-Minus in the Heat, Delaware Bay Gets an A for Croaker
subhead: Warm water has the rips sluggish and spread out, but Fortescue and the bay flats are stacked with croaker, spot, and a surprise run of mackerel.
body_markdown:
If I'm grading the rips this week, it's a C-minus. Fishable, not exciting, and you need to pick your window instead of just showing up and expecting the tide to do the work for you. Water temps on the ocean side have been sitting warm — mid-to-upper 70s at the surface — and that's pushed the bass off the top of the structure and down into whatever cooler water they can find, which this time of year means night bites and the deeper edges around Cape May Point and the outer rip lines. Daytime, the fish are there but they're not stacked and they're not aggressive. This is a classic late-August holding pattern, not the start of the fall run — that push doesn't really get going until the nights start cooling off in earnest, which is usually a mid-September story for us, not a Labor Day one.

Delaware Bay is where the real grade this week is an A. The warm bay water has pulled in the annual southern pulse — croaker, spot, and now a legitimate run of small king mackerel and Spanish mackerel showing up along the beaches from Fortescue down toward the mouth. We flagged this exact pattern building last week and said it would hold as long as bay temps stayed up, and that's exactly what's happened — no cold front has come through to shut it off, so the bite's carried straight through. High-low rigs with bloodworm or fresh clam on size 4 or 2 hooks are the ticket for the croaker and spot, fished right on the bottom off Fortescue and the mouth of the Maurice River. Weakfish are mixing in with those croaker catches, which is a nice bonus — we haven't seen numbers like that on weakies out of the bay in a couple seasons, and most are keeper-class fish in the 16 to 19-inch range, though nobody's limiting out.

The Spanish mackerel showing up is the interesting wrinkle. Small block tin or Clark spoons, trolled behind the jetties on a clean incoming tide, have been connecting for anglers working the surf line and inlet mouths from Cape May up toward Wildwood. These fish follow bait, and as long as that warm plume holds in the bay and along the beachfront, expect them to keep pushing north toward Absecon. The window closes fast the day a real cold front pushes through and knocks the surface water down — so if you want a shot at mackerel on light spinning tackle, don't wait around.

Fluke have taken the hit everywhere this warm spell has touched, and Cape May and Hereford Inlet are no exception. Inside the bay, fluke have spread thin across warm, soft-bottom flats instead of holding tight to structure, which means fewer keepers per drift and a lot more short fish in the mix. The better bet right now is ocean-side — the reef sites and rip structure off Cape May Point where a cooler bottom layer still persists even with warm water up top. Drifting 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, has been the more consistent producer than bare bucktail alone, working the deeper edges of the rip on the last of the ebb and the first hour of the new flood, when current is strongest and bait gets funneled through the troughs.

Bluefish are the one thing you can count on right now, same as everywhere else on this stretch of coast. Snapper blues are thick in the back bay creeks and around the Hereford Inlet docks, and cocktail-sized blues are mixing into both the fluke drifts and the mackerel spoons along the beach. If the rest of the day's slow, a bucktail or metal lip swimmer worked through a blitz of blues will save the trip.

On the black drum — the run that made our name up here wrapped up back in May like it always does, and there's nothing happening on that front worth chasing right now. Anybody asking about drum this week, tell them to circle late April on next year's calendar and be patient.

Looking ahead: the moon builds toward full on Friday, and that's going to strengthen the tidal push through the rips and around Brandywine Shoal — we called this coming last week, and it's the one piece of good news for rip fishermen this stretch. Stronger current means better bait concentration, which should tighten up the bass bite some around the moon, particularly on the night tides at Cape May Point. Weather looks stable through the weekend — southwest wind in the 8 to 12 knot range, no fronts on the immediate horizon — so expect the warm-water pattern in the bay to hold and the croaker/mackerel bite at Fortescue to keep rolling. If a front does slide through behind the full moon, that's when this whole picture flips fast, and the smart move is fishing the bay hard now while it's producing rather than waiting for the ocean side to sort itself out.
